The portal for choosing a major crashed at two, and the deadline was five. Nikita, twenty, grabbed an umbrella and ran across the flooded quad to the registrar's office, a paper form in a plastic sleeve.
In the queue she found her senior, Tanuja. "Still undecided? You've done economics, a term of design, and that rural health survey."
"I know. Everyone says I'm wasting time." Nikita looked at the form. "But on the survey I kept redrawing the charts at midnight because the villagers couldn't read them. Nobody asked me to. It's the only thing I've never got bored of."
"So?"
"So information design. Economics as a minor, for the numbers." She wrote it, rain dripping onto the edge of the paper.
Tanuja grinned. "That took you two years."
"It took two years to know it."

Nilesh, twenty-one, had changed his major twice in two years at the Pune college. Then he'd taken a semester off "to think". Now he was back, sleeping till noon and skipping most classes.
His friend Tanvir found him on the hostel roof. "So what did you figure out, in your semester off?"
Nilesh shrugged. "Nothing much. I watched a lot of stuff. Went to Goa for a week."
"Did you try anything? Talk to anyone?"
"Not really. I'm keeping my options open."
Tanvir sat down. "Open for what?"
Nilesh didn't answer. He looked at the city below. The truth was, the options had been open for two years, and he hadn't walked through any of them. It didn't feel like freedom anymore. It felt like standing still.

Ramesh called today. He asked, "So, what are you now? Still history?"
Honestly, I don't know. First year I, Divyansh, was in physics. Then I switched to history. I spent last summer cycling around Rajasthan and working at a hostel in Jodhpur. This term I joined the debating club and a theatre group.
